messages.subject_clean: 15 minutes missing when analyzing UK biobank raw accelerometer data using GGIR
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I’m trying to extract some physical activity parameters from the UK BioBank raw accelerometer data (AX3, .cwa format) using GGIR package (version 2.3.0). I’m wondering why the starting time of cwa file is different from the GGIR output. 15 minutes are missing of GGIR output. Does anyone has encountered a similar situation? Or maybe our parameter settings are wrong?

Take “accsamp.cwa” as an example.

(Sample datafile of accelerometer results “accsamp.cwa” is downloaded from https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/ukb/refer.cgi?id=131620)

I read the cwa file by g.cwaread function, and it shows that the start time is 2013-07-13 10:00:05.

t <- g.cwaread(fileName = dir, start = 0, end = 10, desiredtz = "Europe/London")

t$header$start

[1] "2013-07-13 10:00:05 BST"

t$data[1:3,]

#         time           x          y          z temp  battery light

# 1 1373706006 -0.67187500  0.1250000 -1.2968750 17.9 4.101562   319

# 2 1373706006 -0.03182551 -0.1099505  0.8454765 17.9 4.101562   319

# 3 1373706006 -0.04572397 -0.1250000  0.8906250 17.9 4.101562   319

library(lubridate)

as_datetime(t$data[1,1], tz = "Europe/London")

# [1] "2013-07-13 10:00:05 BST"

But the start time of the g.shell.GGIR function output is 2013-07-13T10:15:00+0100.

“output_accsamp/meta/csv/accsamp.cwa.RData.csv” file:

The parameters are set as follows.

dir <- "D:/accsamp.cwa"    #cwa file

o.dir <- "D:/"         #output path

name <- "accsamp"

GGIR <- function(d.dir, o.dir, name){

  mode= c(1,2,3,4,5)  # g.part1:5

  datadir= d.dir

  outputdir= o.dir

  studyname= name

  f0 = 1          # number of file to start with

  f1 = 1          # number of file to end with

  desiredtz = "Europe/London"   # time zone

  g.shell.GGIR(#-------------------------------

               # General parameters

               #-------------------------------

               mode=mode,

               datadir=datadir,

               outputdir=outputdir,

               studyname=studyname,

               f0=f0,

               f1=f1,

               overwrite = FALSE,

               do.imp=TRUE,

               idloc=1,

               print.filename=FALSE,

               storefolderstructure = FALSE,

               desiredtz=desiredtz,

               #start = 0,

               #dayborder = 10,

               #-------------------------------

               # Part 1 parameters:

               #-------------------------------

               windowsizes = c(5,900,3600),

               desiredtz=desiredtz,

               do.cal=TRUE,

               do.enmo=TRUE,

               do.anglez=TRUE,

               chunksize=1.5,

               printsummary=TRUE,

               do.hfen = FALSE,

               #-------------------------------

               # Part 2 parameters:

               #-------------------------------

               strategy = 1,

               #ndayswindow = nday,

               hrs.del.start = 0,

               hrs.del.end = 0,

               maxdur = 0,

               includedaycrit = 2,

               M5L5res = 10,

               winhr = c(5,10),

               qlevels = c(0.25,0.5,0.75),

               qwindow=c(0,24),

               ilevels = c(0,100,200),

               mvpathreshold =c(100,120),

               epochvalues2csv=TRUE,

               L5M5window = c(0,24),

               #-------------------------------

               # Part 3 parameters:

               #-------------------------------

               timethreshold= c(5),

               anglethreshold=5,

               ignorenonwear = TRUE,

               #-------------------------------

               # Part 4 parameters:

               #-------------------------------

               excludefirstlast = FALSE,

               includenightcrit = 2,

               def.noc.sleep = c(1),

               outliers.only = FALSE,

               criterror= 0,

               relyonsleeplog = FALSE,

               sleeplogidnum = FALSE,

               do.visual = TRUE,

               nnights = c(),

               excludefirstlast = FALSE,

               #-------------------------------

               # Part 5 parameters:

               #-------------------------------

               # Key functions: Merging physical activity with sleep analyses

               excludefirstlast.part5 =FALSE,

               threshold.lig = c(30),

               threshold.mod = c(100),

               threshold.vig = c(500),

               boutcriter = 0.8,

               boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,

               boutcriter.lig = 0.8,

               boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8,

               boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(1,10,30),

               boutdur.lig = c(1,5,10),

               boutdur.mvpa = c(1,5,10),

               timewindow = c("WW"),

               #save_ms5rawlevels=FALSE

               #includedaycrit.part5 = 0.1,

               #-----------------------------------

               # Report generation

               #-------------------------------

               do.report=c(2,4,5),

               visualreport=TRUE,

               viewingwindow=1)

}

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Processing without resampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

This is not possible at the moment.
The next processing steps in GGIR requires as input a time series with constant sampling frequency. It would require substantial code modifications to make GGIR skip the resampling.

Best regards, Vincent

messages.subject: A question about applying daylight saving function
messages.subject_clean: A question about applying daylight saving function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I wonder if anyone has the experience using is_this_a_dst_night function to test if the night that follows the input calendar date is a night with day saving time (DST) and on what hour the time moved. I have some data from Actigraph accelerometers. But the Actigraph accelerometers were worn past the night with day saving time (DST) (for example, We were at the EST timezone and daylight saving time 2020 ended at 2:00 AM on Nov 1st. We had some participant who wore it from Oct 25th to Nov 5th, which the wearing time crossed the daylight saving changing day).

Can is_this_a_dst_night function solve this kind of questions? What would be the best solution to deal with the data like that?

Thanks,
Julia

This is surely some dumb thing, but I just cannot figure it out!

Thank you all for any suggestion or hint.

messages.subject: Re: How Do I Report Average MVPA, LPA, and Inactivity Time (in Minutes/Day)?
messages.subject_clean: How Do I Report Average MVPA, LPA, and Inactivity Time (in Minutes/Day)?
messages.body_plain:
If you are only after these variables you might as well use part2 only. assuming based on the filename you gave that you used something like the argument ilevels = c(0,30,100,400,8000).

if so, you can get the time spent in minutes in columns in part2_daysummary
[30,100)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr
[100,400)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr
[400,8e+03)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr

or part2_summary for average over all valid days
AD_[30,100)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr
AD_[100,400)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr
AD_[400,8e+03)_ENMO_mg_0-24hr

The above assumes that you have done all the necessary QC checks on the data beyond the GGIR checks.

Hope that helps,
Ben

Regarding your question:

All steps related to taking into account study design, such as argument 'strategy', and the imputation of invalid data take place in part 2 of GGIR. I recommend using function g.shell.GGIR as that would avoid having to think which function argument needs to be set for which GGIR part.

- non-wear
- time segments ignored because of study protocol, e.g. ignore first and last day.
- detected signal clipping, this should be very rare.

The GGIR reports come with columns that indicate the amount of valid/invalid data per day or per recording.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Chian-Heng,

GGIR aggregates data per short, medium and long epoch. The default for these are 5, 900 and 3600 seconds respectively. The short epoch is used for quantifying behaviour, while the medium and long epochs are used for detecting non-wear detection.

To ease comparisons between recordings these epochs are extracted in a way that all medium length epochs align with the hour. So, if your recording starts at 10:07, the GGIR will extract epochs from 10:15 onward, because that is the next 900 second (15 minutes) point in the hour.

If you want to shorten this poch length then to let's say 300 seconds, then that is fine. I do not see any danger with that in terms of non-wear detection accuracy. The only disadvantage is that it could slow down GGIR a bit.

Best, Vincent

That function is used by GGIR internally, as a user you should not have to worry about it.
So, if all goes well GGIR automatically takes in account DST.

In GGIR part 2 output you should see this in the fact that DST nights will results in 25 or 23 measurement hours in a day. Further, in the part 4 output you will notice that when sleep starts before DST and ends after DST it will one hour more or one hour less in sleep duration compared to what you would expect from the start and end clock time.

Did you encounter any data that gave doubt that this is correctly working?
If you did, then please let me know.

It means that if a day window lasts for 24 hours and includedaycrit.part5 = 2/3 = 0.6666
we require at least 16 valid hours of data (24 x 0.666 = 16).

WW windows are usually not exactly 24 hours, so this means that the criteria on the required number of valid hours changes proportionally. For example, with a day of 18 hours, the required number of valid hours becomes 12 (18 x 0.666 = 12), while for a day of 30 hours, the required number of valid hours becomes 20.

Does this clarify your question?

Hi Claire,

Good to hear from you. My responses to your questions are below in red:

1. In the validation paper, it mentions that this algorithm can be used for data collected from wrist worn devices. I wanted to check if this algorithm can also be used for non-wrist worn devices (thigh/waist etc...)

MP: Unfortunately, the algorithm has not been tested out on data from the thigh or waist. Ideally, a validation study would be done to assess the performance. My intuition is that it might not work out that well, as the acceleration experienced during an arm swing is higher than is normally seen at the waist or the thigh. However, you could try applying it to data and see if the results look like they are reasonable.

2. Will this algorithm also work for data collected from children? Or is there anything that would be needed to be taken into consideration (e.g changing certain parameters) when processing child data?

MP: The participants in the original work were adults only, so it is not known how the algorithm would work on children. It is not known if it is possible to change the parameters to get the algorithm working on children. Again, you could try applying it to some pilot data to see how it works.

MP: The algorithm was created on data from adults who were wearing the sensor at the wrist, so any deviation from this mounting location and population means that it is not known how the algorithm will behave. My intuition is that changing populations wouldn't cause as much problems as changing locations, as the algorithm was created with unstructured walking bouts. This probably isn't the answer you were hoping for, but it is the current state of the algorithm. Let me know if you have any other questions.

All the best,

Matt
